description: How Greeks and Romans worshipped — prayer, votive offerings, libations and the ritual of animal sacrifice.
content_html:
Religion in Everyday Life

For the ancient Greeks and Romans, religion was not a Sunday activity or a private matter — it was woven into every aspect of daily life. Before eating, a Greek might pour a few drops of wine on the ground as a libation to the gods. Before a sea voyage, a Roman would sacrifice at a temple. When something important happened — a birth, a victory in battle, a safe return — the pious response was to honour the deity responsible. The gods were understood as active presences whose goodwill had to be maintained through regular acts of piety.

Prayer and Votive Offerings

Prayer in the ancient world had a distinctive physical dimension. Greek worshippers typically stood upright, raised their arms with palms facing upward towards the sky when addressing the Olympians, or turned them downward towards the earth when addressing gods of the underworld. Roman worshippers often covered their heads with a fold of their toga — the capite velato gesture — during prayer and sacrifice, symbolising reverence and the blocking out of bad omens.

Alongside prayer, worshippers made votive offerings. These ranged from small terracotta figurines and clay models of the body part healed (a foot, a hand, an eye) to expensive bronze tripods and silver vessels. Sanctuaries across the Greek world were filled with accumulated offerings, creating a visible record of the community’s gratitude. At the Sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, for example, stone tablets described miraculous cures, and model limbs were left in thanksgiving. The practice reflects the reciprocal logic of ancient religion: the worshipper gave something in exchange for the god’s favour.

Key Fact

Votive offerings could include terracotta figurines, model body parts, bronze vessels, weapons, jewellery or painted tablets. They expressed reciprocity — the worshipper’s side of the exchange with the deity. A fulfilled promise to dedicate an offering was called a vow in Latin; Roman temples accumulated wealth through the objects left by grateful worshippers.

Animal Sacrifice: The Central Act of Worship

Animal sacrifice was the most important and elaborate form of worship in both Greek and Roman culture. The logic was the same as with votive offerings — giving the most valuable thing possible to the gods — but sacrifice was a public, communal event that could involve hundreds of people and was closely tied to civic festivals.

In a Greek sacrifice, the animal had to be perfect and unblemished: a bull, ox, cow, sheep, goat or pig, depending on the deity and the occasion. The animal was led in procession to the altar, adorned with garlands and gilded horns for a major sacrifice. Water was sprinkled on its head, and barley grains were scattered — the animal shaking its head was interpreted as a sign of willingness. The sacrificer (who might be a priest, a magistrate, or even a general before battle) then struck the animal with an axe or stunned it before cutting its throat over the altar.

The blood was collected and poured over the altar — the altar received the god’s share. The internal organs, especially the liver and lungs, were inspected for omens (see the next lesson on divination). The thighbones were wrapped in fat and burned on the altar fire, producing the smoke that the gods were believed to find pleasing. The rest of the meat was roasted and eaten by the worshippers, making sacrifice simultaneously a religious act, a communal feast, and one of the few occasions on which ordinary Greeks ate meat.

Roman sacrifice followed a broadly similar pattern but with distinctive features. The sacrificing magistrate covered his head (capite velato) and was accompanied by specialists: a haruspex to examine the entrails, and musicians playing flutes to drown out any bad omens heard during the rite. The animals most commonly sacrificed in public Roman ritual were the bull, sheep and pig together — a ceremony known as the suovetaurilia, used for major occasions such as the purification of the army.

A critical difference: the Romans demanded absolute ritual correctness. If the priest made a mistake — mispronounced a word, broke the silence, or the animal escaped — the entire sacrifice had to be repeated from the start. This principle of piacula (atonement) meant that religious officials were extremely careful and that the procedures were highly formalised compared to Greek practice.

Key Fact

The four main stages of a Greek animal sacrifice: (1) Procession — the animal led adorned to the altar; (2) Preparation — water and barley scattered, the animal’s “consent” obtained; (3) Killing — the animal killed at the altar, blood poured over it; (4) Division — thighbones and fat burned for the gods; meat roasted and shared by the community.

Household Worship

Public sacrifice and temple ritual were not the only forms of worship. Both Greeks and Romans maintained religious practice in the home. Greek households kept a small hearth sacred to Hestia, and daily libations were poured to household gods at meals. Roman households maintained a small shrine called a lararium, where statuettes of the Lares (household guardian spirits) and the Penates (gods of the storeroom) were kept. The head of the household, the paterfamilias, conducted daily rituals at this shrine, including burning incense and offering food. This domestic piety was considered just as important as participation in public cult.

A key concept underpinning all ancient worship is the Latin phrase do ut des — “I give so that you may give.” The relationship between worshipper and deity was conceived as a reciprocal transaction: you honoured the god with prayer, sacrifice and offerings, and in return the god was expected to provide protection, good harvests, victory or health. This is very different from modern conceptions of prayer as purely spiritual or non-transactional. The gods of Greece and Rome were not morally perfect beings who demanded good behaviour from their worshippers — they wanted the correct rituals performed correctly, and regularly.
exam_tip_html: The command word Describe in this topic often appears as “Describe how a Greek sacrifice was carried out.” Give a step-by-step account: what happened before, during and after. Do not just say “they killed an animal” — name the specific stages (procession, preparation, killing, division of the carcass) and explain what each stage involved. The most common mistake is focusing only on the killing and forgetting the communal meal at the end, which is often just as important as evidence for the social function of sacrifice. For source-analysis questions, if you are given a description of a sacrifice scene, use specific visual details: who is shown, what objects appear (altar, axe, garlands, fire), and what the position of the figures suggests about the ritual’s social meaning.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ancient Greek and Roman worship operated on a “do ut des” (give-to-receive) model: prayer, libations and votive offerings expressed piety and maintained the gods’ goodwill in return for protection and favour.
  • Animal sacrifice was the central public act of worship: the gods received the bones and fat burned on the altar fire, while the community shared the roasted meat — making sacrifice a communal feast as well as a religious rite.
  • Roman sacrifice placed greater emphasis on ritual precision (the haruspex, correct formulae, absolute silence); any error required the whole ceremony to be repeated from the beginning.

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a liquid offering (wine, water, milk or oil) poured out as an act of worship to the gods.

practice_questions.text: Describe how an animal sacrifice was carried out in ancient Greece.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: the animal was led in procession to the altar adorned with garlands; water and barley grains were scattered and the animal's 'consent' obtained; the animal was killed at the altar and the blood poured over it; the internal organs were inspected for omens; the thighbones and fat were burned on the altar fire as the gods' share; the remaining meat was roasted and eaten by the community.

practice_questions.text: Consider this description of a scene painted on a Greek vessel: a procession of figures approaches a stone altar; the leading figure holds a vessel from which liquid is being poured onto the altar's surface, while others carry garlands; in the background an ox is being led forward with gilded horns. What does this scene tell us about how the Greeks worshipped? Use specific details from the description in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5): Uses multiple specific details from the description (liquid poured on altar = libation; garlands on figures and gilded horns on ox = ceremonial preparation; procession = communal public event) with sustained analysis linking each to what it reveals about Greek religious attitudes (reciprocity, spectacle, community, the god's share vs the people's share). Judgement clearly expressed.
Secure (3-4): Two or three details analysed with clear explanation of significance.
Developing (2): One or two details mentioned with limited analysis.
Emerging (1): General description of sacrifice without engaging with source details.

practice_questions.text: Explain why animal sacrifice was so important in both Greek and Roman religion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any four of the following: sacrifice was the most valuable gift a worshipper could give, reflecting the 'do ut des' logic; it was a public communal event that reinforced civic bonds; it provided meat for the community, making it an important social occasion; it gave religious officials an opportunity to read omens from the entrails; it maintained the gods' goodwill through regular, correct performance of ritual; it was tied to festivals and calendar events so structured the religious year.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that animal sacrifice was the most important form of worship in the ancient Greek and Roman world? Use a range of named sources and a balanced argument.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9-10): Sustained balanced argument weighing sacrifice (public ritual, meat feast, divination, civic bonding) against other forms of worship (household lararium, votive offerings, prayer, libations) with specific named examples; awareness that 'importance' can mean different things (public vs private piety; elite vs everyday worshipper); judgement clearly supported by named sources and evidence.
Secure (6-8): Clear argument covering at least two forms of worship with named evidence and a conclusion.
Developing (3-5): Some relevant points; limited comparison or limited source use.
Emerging (1-2): Simple descriptive points; little argument.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Greek and Roman animal sacrifice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Two clearly explained differences (e.g. Roman priest covered head capite velato vs Greek bare-headed; Roman haruspex examined entrails formally vs Greek more informal; Roman demand for ritual perfection and repetition if error vs Greek less rigid; suovetaurilia in Rome vs more varied animals in Greece) each with a named example and a clear sense of what the difference reveals about each culture's attitudes to the gods.
Secure (3-4): Two differences explained with some evidence.
Developing (1-2): One difference stated or two superficially mentioned.

knowledge_checks.q: In a Roman sacrifice, what was the role of the haruspex?
options: To lead the sacrificial animal in procession
To play music during the ceremony
To examine the entrails of the animal for divine signs
To distribute the meat to the community

knowledge_checks.q: In a Greek sacrifice, the thighbones and fat were burned on the altar fire as the _____'s share, while the remaining meat was eaten by the community.
The Latin phrase 'do ut des' describes the reciprocal logic of ancient worship: 'I give so that you may _____.'
Match each term to its correct description:
right: A liquid offering poured out as an act of worship to the gods
An object dedicated at a sanctuary in thanks for a divine favour
Greek goddess of the hearth, whose flame was kept in every household

flashcard_questions.q: What is a libation in ancient Greek and Roman religion?
flashcard_questions.a: A liquid offering (wine, water, milk or oil) poured out as an act of worship to the gods.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Latin phrase that describes the reciprocal logic of ancient worship?
flashcard_questions.a: Do ut des — 'I give so that you may give.'

flashcard_questions.q: What did a worshipper leave at a sanctuary as a gift to the gods?
flashcard_questions.a: A votive offering — such as a terracotta figurine, model body part, or bronze vessel.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the thighbones and fat in a Greek animal sacrifice?
flashcard_questions.a: They were burned on the altar fire as the god's share.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the remaining meat after the gods' portion was burned in Greek sacrifice?
flashcard_questions.a: It was roasted and shared as a communal meal by the worshippers.

flashcard_questions.q: What Roman specialist examined the entrails of sacrificial animals for divine signs?
What gesture did a Roman priest make during sacrifice to show reverence and block out bad omens?
flashcard_questions.a: He covered his head with a fold of his toga — capite velato.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the suovetaurilia in Roman religion?
flashcard_questions.a: The sacrifice of a bull, sheep and pig together, used for major purification ceremonies.

flashcard_questions.q: What was a lararium in a Roman home?
flashcard_questions.a: A small household shrine where statuettes of the Lares and Penates were kept.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Greek goddess was associated with the sacred hearth fire kept in every household?
Why did Roman ritual have to be repeated from the beginning if an error was made?
flashcard_questions.a: Romans required absolute ritual correctness; any mistake invalidated the ceremony.

flashcard_questions.q: What did a worshipper's physical posture during prayer in ancient Greece involve?
flashcard_questions.a: Standing upright with arms raised, palms facing upward towards the Olympian gods.

glossary_terms.definition: A liquid offering poured out as an act of worship, typically wine, water, milk or oil, either onto the ground or into a fire.
An object dedicated and left at a sanctuary as a gift to the gods in thanks for a favour received or in hope of one to come.
The ritual killing of an animal at an altar as an offering to the gods, the central act of public worship in both Greek and Roman religion.
A Roman specialist in divination who examined the entrails of sacrificed animals, particularly the liver, for signs from the gods.
The Greek goddess of the hearth and home, whose sacred flame was maintained in every household and in the communal hearth of each city.
